sections.b:
On the tenth day of the month, "at the start of the year" (spring or autumn: the text does not say), in 573 BC, a shining guide with a linen cord and a measuring reed leads Ezekiel through the new Temple. He measures the outer wall, three outer gates, the outer court, three inner gates, the inner court, the porch, the great hall, the innermost room (a cube of twenty cubits), the priests' rooms and a wall around the whole area. The unit is a long cubit of about 52 cm.

The plan keeps the holy apart from the ordinary (42:20). It has no ark in the innermost room, no lampstand and no bronze Sea. The glory of the LORD comes back through the east gate and fills the house (43:1-5), and the chapters end with the rules for the altar's seven-day dedication (43:18-27).

common: The vision is dated to 573 BC and is the last dated vision in Ezekiel.
uncommon: The measurements were meant as a drawing for builders; most readers, Jewish and Christian, have not taken the plan this way.

sections.h: Ezekiel's Temple: the house that the glory fills
sections.b: Ezekiel's Temple stands on a very high mountain (40:2). Its main hall and innermost room have Solomon's proportions (1 Kings 6:17, 20), and its walls carry cherubim and palm trees (41:18-20). It differs from every Temple that was built. Its outer wall and gates make the holy area a square of 500 on each side (42:15-20); its innermost room is empty of furniture in the account; its altar has steps (43:17). Jews and Christians have read it as a plan to be built, as an ideal, as the church or Christ, and as the new creation. See the page on Ezekiel's Temple Vision.

sections.h: The glory returns to the Temple (Ezekiel 43:1-5)
sections.b: The glory of the LORD that left the Temple toward the east (Ezekiel 10:18-19; 11:22-23) comes back from the east, with a sound like many waters, and enters the new house by the east gate. It fills the house as it filled the Tabernacle (Exodus 40:34-35) and Solomon's Temple (1 Kings 8:10-11). This is the climax of Ezekiel, who first saw the glory at the Kebar canal (1:28) and falls on his face again (43:3). The rabbis said the Second Temple lacked the glory (Yoma 21b), and Christians see its return in Jesus (John 1:14) and in the new Jerusalem (Revelation 21:22-23).
sections.refs: Ezekiel 43:1-5; Ezekiel 1:28; Ezekiel 10:18-19; Ezekiel 11:22-23; Exodus 40:34-35; 1 Kings 8:10-11; John 1:14; Revelation 21:22-23

sections.b: Ezekiel names the sons of Zadok as the priests who "keep watch over the altar" and come near the LORD to serve him (40:46). The sin-offering bull for the altar's dedication is given to "the Levite priests who are of the offspring of Zadok" (43:19). Chapter 44 explains why they, and not the other Levites, hold the altar. Zadok served David and anointed Solomon (1 Kings 1:32-39), and his family held the high priesthood in the Temple.

Tables at the inner gates are for killing the burnt offering, the sin offering and the guilt offering (40:38-43). The altar is dedicated over seven days: a bull as a sin offering on day one, a male goat on each of the following days, and a bull and a ram as burnt offerings (43:18-27). The rules differ from Exodus 29:35-37 and Leviticus 8 (a goat, not a bull, each day). Christians divide on whether any such offerings will be offered again; see the card at Ezekiel 43:18-27. The Talmud says the sages nearly shelved the book because its laws seemed to contradict the Torah (Shabbat 13b).

The walls of Ezekiel's house are carved with cherubim between palm trees, each cherub with two faces, a human and a young lion. They are guardians of a garden-like house, like the cherubim carved in Solomon's Temple (1 Kings 6:29). They are not the living creatures of chapters 1 and 10, who have four faces (1:10; 10:14).

Two blocks of rooms, north and south of the house, are the place where the priests eat the most holy offerings (42:13; compare Leviticus 6:16-18), store them, and change out of their service clothes before going out among the people (42:14; compare 44:19). The point is that holy things and holy clothes pass holiness on, and must stay in a holy place.

sections.h: The wall that separates the holy from the ordinary (Ezekiel 42:20)
sections.b: The wall around the Temple area exists, the text says, "to separate the holy from the ordinary" (42:20), the duty of the priests in Leviticus 10:10 which Ezekiel 22:26 says they had neglected. In 43:12 the whole mountaintop is called most holy, not just the innermost room.

In the vision the LORD speaks from the house and says it is the place of his throne and the soles of his feet, where he will live among the Israelites forever. The ark had been his footstool (1 Chronicles 28:2; Psalm 99:5); Ezekiel's vision does not mention it, and the LORD's own glory takes its place.

sections.h: Cleansing and atonement for the altar (Ezekiel 43:20, 26)
sections.b: The altar itself is cleansed from sin and atoned for by blood on its horns, ledge and rim (43:20), and for seven days it is atoned for again (43:26). The sin offering here cleans a holy object, not a person; Jacob Milgrom argued that this is what the sin offering does in the law of Moses.

sections.h: The tenth day of the month in 573 BC (Ezekiel 40:1)
sections.b: The rabbis read "the start of the year, the tenth day of the month" as the tenth of Tishri, the Day of Atonement, and counted that year as a Jubilee (Rosh Hashanah 8b; Arakhin 12a). The text itself does not say. If the year began in spring, the date is the tenth of Nisan.

sections.h: Kings and high places in Ezekiel 43:7-9
sections.b: The LORD says Israel's house and its kings defiled his name "by their prostitution and by the corpses of their kings on their high places" (43:7). The words are disputed: royal tombs near the Temple, a cult of dead kings, a word for idols, or "at their death". See the note at 43:7.

Ezekiel's vision begins on "a very high mountain" with "something like the buildings of a city" to the south. Revelation 21:10 takes the same picture: the angel carries John to a great, high mountain to see the holy city, but the city has no temple (Revelation 21:22).

sections.h: Rooms for singers in the Hebrew of Ezekiel 40:44
sections.b: The Hebrew of Ezekiel 40:44 calls the two rooms in the inner court "rooms for singers", one beside the north gate and one beside the east gate (the Greek has the second beside the south gate). The Greek has "two rooms" and no word for singers, and 40:45-46 give the same two rooms to the priests, so the singers belong to the Hebrew text of that verse only. Ezekiel does not mention singers again in these chapters. Levite singers served David's Temple (1 Chronicles 25:1-7) and returned from the exile (Ezra 2:41).

Ezekiel's innermost room is a cube of twenty cubits, as in Solomon's Temple, but the description gives its measurements only: no ark, no mercy seat and no cherubim above it. Jeremiah 3:16 says the ark would no longer be remembered; Ezekiel 43:7 puts the LORD's own throne in its place.
